title: How Reverse Psychology Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore reverse psychology: telling someone to do the opposite of what you want so they do it. They cover psychological reactance (people asserting autonomy by opposing pressure), negative reverse psychology in parenting (e.g., insulting a child to get a chore done), why it can teach kids not to trust parents, and personality traits (Type A, narcissism, control freaks) that may make people more susceptible. They discuss research on children and toys (a motorcycle children were told not to play with became more desirable), curiosity versus autonomy explanations (Esther Inglis-Arkell's "forbidden" door example), teen cheating experiments, sales and relationship examples, paradoxical intervention as a real therapy (e.g., scheduled procrastination), compliance techniques (door-in-the-face, foot-in-the-door), and the healthy approach of openly respecting someone's autonomy. The episode ends with listener mail from Robbie about his "three favorite things" experiment.

segments.title: Opening banter and manipulation in relationships
segments.summary: Josh opens by saying he is grumpy about the topic and dislikes manipulative relationship games, citing an ex-boyfriend recovery site. Chuck and Josh discuss toxic relationships and honesty, then introduce reverse psychology and the psychological concept of reactance.

segments.title: Reverse psychology examples and parenting
segments.summary: The hosts give examples of reverse psychology between spouses (painting a bedroom) and parents, including negative reverse psychology such as insulting a child to get a bike hung up. They warn that overuse teaches kids not to trust or listen to parents, and describe the long-hair example.

segments.title: Who is susceptible: personality and context
segments.summary: Experts suggest narcissists, control freaks and Type A personalities may be more susceptible, since the technique depends on threatened autonomy. Type B people may just do what is asked. Psychologist Janette Raymond and a 2011 Psychology Today piece argue relationship dynamics and context matter, with Charlie Sheen's rehab as an example.

segments.title: Children, toys and reactance research
segments.summary: Children tend to want what they are told they cannot have. Studies described had children rate toys; the middle-ranked motorcycle became more desirable after being forbidden. Hosts note adults do the same, including with advertising such as a Patagonia ad saying not to buy the jacket.

segments.title: Curiosity versus autonomy and the forbidden door
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether reactance comes from rebelling against authority or from piqued curiosity. Esther Inglis-Arkell's forbidden door and toilet overflow example illustrates curiosity. A teen cheating study found that telling students not to cheat increased cheating. Examples include Tom and Jerry and The Simpsons, and the Google image warnings about disturbing medical content.

segments.title: Sales, relationships, and paradoxical intervention
segments.summary: Examples from car sales and dating are given. The hosts then describe paradoxical intervention, a real therapy where patients are told to deliberately perform a symptom, such as scheduled procrastination. They discuss its ethics, noting it is manipulative if the patient does not know the technique.

segments.title: Compliance techniques and respecting autonomy
segments.summary: The hosts define door-in-the-face and foot-in-the-door compliance techniques, referencing MPAA ratings. They describe a healthier approach of explicitly stating the person's autonomy, and mention the Door in the Floor film and John Irving's A Widow for One Year.

segments.title: Listener mail: Robbie's three favorite things
segments.summary: Robbie, an artist who listens while painting, shares his street experiment asking New Yorkers for their three favorite things (family, music, food). The hosts answer the question and the episode closes with ways to contact the show.
